message.reasoning:
I need to make a decision for this Monopoly turn.

I have $3,266 and four full houses on the light blues. The opponent has only $34 and heavy investments in dark blues. I am considering whether to trade, unmortgage, or build.

The bank has only five houses left. I am recalculating rent and liquidity to decide whether to trade, unmortgage, or build.

Standard Monopoly rent for four houses on the pinks is $625 per property. The current game schedule shows $700 on Virginia Avenue, so I am verifying the exact rent schedule before deciding whether to hotel.

Standard Monopoly Virginia rent with four houses is $900. Hotels would cost $100–300 but only raise rent by $125–200. The opponent would gain four houses back from the bank for each hotel built.

I am reconsidering the freeze strategy. If the bank has no houses, the opponent cannot sell hotels or houses because they need four houses to replace them. I need to verify whether this game returns houses when selling a hotel.

The bank has five houses remaining. The opponent can still break one hotel by downgrading it to four houses and selling them. Connecticut Avenue is the likely target.

The opponent just paid $700 rent on Virginia Avenue. That drained their cash to $34. They had to liquidate red properties and sell the Boardwalk hotel to cover it. Their current liquidity is now very tight.

I can easily cover any rent I might face. Park Place with four houses would cost $1,300, and Boardwalk with three houses is well below the hotel rate. The opponent's liquidity problems are their own to solve on their turn.

Hoteling all three pinks would return twelve houses to the bank. That would leave the opponent with seventeen houses and fully unlock their liquidation options. The freeze strategy is losing value because they can already break one hotel.

Selling houses returns them to the bank. Only hotels require four houses in the bank to downgrade or sell. The opponent can freely sell Boardwalk and Park Place houses. They cannot break a second hotel without four more houses.

I am now estimating the opponent's total liquidation value. Boardwalk houses sell for $300, Park Place for $400, and the light blues for roughly $200 combined. The Connecticut hotel must be downgraded to four houses first.

I am reconsidering the house-return mechanics. Standard rules say selling a hotel returns half its cost and requires four replacement houses from the bank. I need to verify whether this game actually returns houses when selling hotels, or if the bank must hold four houses before any downgrade is possible.

Even-build rules freeze light-blue and Park Place houses too. The opponent cannot sell those properties until they break the Connecticut hotel first. Boardwalk now has three houses, so they can sell it freely.

The opponent can now sell dark blue houses freely. They can sell one house from Park Place to even the count, then sell the remaining five for $700 total. After downgrading the Connecticut hotel, they will also be able to sell all light blue houses.

I am working out the exact cash value of demolishing the Connecticut hotel. A light blue hotel costs $50, so selling it would return roughly $25. I am weighing whether the player keeps four houses or receives $125 and must place four houses elsewhere.

The opponent now has roughly $734 in liquid assets, more than enough to cover the $700 Virginia rent. They just landed on that property and survived by selling reds and the Boardwalk hotel.

I am mapping the opponent's next roll from Virginia Avenue. The standard board order after that space is Pennsylvania Railroad, St. James Place, Community Chest, St. Charles Place, Electric Company, States Avenue, and then back to Virginia Avenue.

The standard board order after Virginia Avenue is now mapped. Rolling a two lands on St. James Place, which is mortgaged and owned by the opponent. A roll of three brings them to Community Chest. A roll of four would reach Tennessee Avenue, which is mortgaged and owned by me.

The opponent's next rolls from Virginia Avenue will not land on any of my pink properties. New York, Kentucky, Indiana, Illinois, B&O, and Atlantic are all owned by the opponent and mortgaged. The first pink property they will reach is St. Charles Place, which requires going completely around the board.

The opponent must roll 33 spaces to reach St. Charles Place from Virginia Avenue. A maximum roll of 12 cannot cover that distance, so they will not land on a pink property this turn.

The opponent could theoretically reach St. Charles Place from Virginia Avenue in one turn by rolling two doubles followed by a high non-double roll, covering 35 spaces. This is unlikely but possible.

I am now mapping the spaces immediately ahead of my position on Electric Company. The next spaces are States Avenue, Virginia Avenue, Pennsylvania Railroad, St. James Place, Community Chest, Tennessee Avenue, New York Avenue, Free Parking, Kentucky Avenue, Chance, and Indiana Avenue.

The opponent cannot land on any of my improved properties this turn. Park Place is 25 spaces away and Boardwalk is 27. Even with two doubles, the maximum roll is only about 35.

I realized the opponent cannot land on Park Place this turn. Two doubles sum to an even number, but 25 is odd, so they cannot reach that space without a third roll.

I am now checking whether the opponent can land on any of my improved properties from Electric Company. Even with one double, their total movement would only reach 4 to 24 spaces, which is still too short to reach any of my light-blue or dark-blue properties.

Oriental Avenue is 30 spaces away, so the opponent cannot land there this turn. Reaching it would require two doubles plus a high non-double roll, totaling 35 spaces.

The opponent cannot land on any of my improved properties this turn. The probability of two doubles followed by a high non-double roll is only about two percent, so that scenario is not worth optimizing for.

I am now weighing whether to build hotels on the pink properties. Each hotel would increase rent by roughly one hundred twenty-five to one hundred seventy-five dollars per hit, and I have three thousand two hundred sixty-six dollars in cash, so the cost is easily manageable.

Building three hotels would return twelve houses to the bank. That fully unlocks the opponent's ability to sell both hotels and rebuild. The opponent currently has only thirty-four dollars in cash, so they cannot afford new construction. However, having more houses in the bank would let them liquidate properties more freely to survive my rent demands.

The house freeze is already mostly broken. The bank holds five houses, so the opponent can already liquidate both hotels and rebuild. Extra houses do not unlock additional hotel sales.

Hotel construction costs three hundred dollars but only raises rent by four hundred twenty-five dollars across the full board. The opponent must circle the board to hit these properties, so the expected value is weak. I am now checking whether St. Charles Place sits immediately after Connecticut Avenue.

St. Charles Place is directly adjacent to Connecticut Avenue. The opponent will pass through the pink zone from the light blues, so any landing there pays rent. Hotels would pay for themselves if they land on these properties twice or three times over a long game. Higher rent might also bankrupt them before they can fully liquidate. Dark blue houses sell for one hundred dollars each.

The opponent's total liquid assets are roughly one thousand one hundred to one thousand two hundred dollars. Dark blue houses sell for four hundred dollars, and light blue houses sell for three hundred dollars. The four-house rents on the pink properties are six hundred twenty-five, six hundred twenty-five, and seven hundred dollars.

Hotel rent on Virginia Avenue would be eight hundred seventy-five dollars. The opponent cannot survive that with only dark blue liquidation; they would need light blue assets as well. Hotel rent on St. Charles Place or States Avenue would be seven hundred fifty dollars, which they could barely afford without selling light blues.

Hotels would force the opponent to liquidate all buildings to survive Virginia Avenue rent. They cannot reach me for a full circuit, so they will collect $200 from GO and land on their own properties or Chance. With only $34 in cash plus that $200, they could afford one dark blue house and even out Boardwalk.

The opponent has only thirty-four dollars in cash. They cannot afford new construction unless they sell buildings, collect two hundred dollars from passing GO, or receive money from me. Leaving the bank at five houses would keep them cash-poor and unable to rebuild.

The opponent can still break one hotel and sell houses. The five-house bank limit remains the key constraint. Selling houses returns them to the bank, so the opponent can rebuild later. Building now is difficult because they already own many properties.

Oriental and Vermont are fully built at four houses each. Hoteling them would return eight houses to the bank, but that costs fifty dollars per hotel and the opponent only has thirty-four dollars. The dark blues currently have four and three houses respectively.

The opponent cannot afford to buy a single dark blue house with only thirty-four dollars. After collecting two hundred dollars from passing GO, they would have two hundred thirty-four dollars and could purchase one Boardwalk house. The five-house bank limit does not block this because cash is the real constraint. Selling buildings returns houses to the bank, so house scarcity never prevents them from rebuilding later.

Hoteling would not unlock new construction for the opponent, since they lack cash. The downside is small. The upside is higher rent and a greater chance of bankrupting them. Virginia Avenue's eight hundred seventy-five-dollar hotel rent exceeds their maximum liquidity. They might accumulate more cash by passing GO or drawing Chance cards before eventually landing on the pinks. Reaching St. Charles Place from Electric Company requires roughly thirty-three spaces, which averages about five turns.

The opponent will likely reach my pink properties with only about two hundred thirty-four dollars in cash, since mortgaged properties pay no rent and their other income is limited to passing GO. That amount is below the six hundred twenty-five-dollar rent on St. Charles Place, so they cannot survive without selling buildings. I should set rent above their maximum liquidation capacity before they land. I will now check whether my prior strategy conclusion still holds.

The opponent already sold the Boardwalk hotel and broke the Connecticut Avenue hotel. The bank now holds five houses, so they can break the last remaining hotel themselves. The argument that hoteling would unlock their hotels is weaker now because only one hotel remains.

Virginia Avenue hotel rent would now exceed the opponent's dark-blue-only liquidity of seven hundred thirty-four dollars. That forces them to liquidate light blue properties as well, removing their main rent threat against me.

The game's rent scaling appears close to standard values. Virginia's four-house rent of seven hundred dollars versus standard nine hundred suggests a scale factor near seventy-eight percent.

Standard house values are one hundred fifty dollars each, with a seventy-five-dollar sell-back. The opponent can liquidate their properties for roughly half their purchase price.

I am now estimating the opponent's exact sell-back values. Their dark blue properties would return roughly seven hundred dollars total, while their light blue properties would return about four hundred eighty-five dollars. I am also calculating how much cash they could raise by selling individual buildings, such as four houses on Pennsylvania Railroad or three houses on Boardwalk.

The opponent's dark blue properties would return roughly nine hundred dollars if fully liquidated. Selling the Boardwalk hotel yields five houses, or about five hundred dollars. Adding four houses on Pennsylvania Railroad brings the total to nine hundred dollars.

The opponent can fully liquidate all buildings. The bank holds five houses, so they can sell the Connecticut Avenue hotel and even-build to sell light blue houses. Their total liquid assets are roughly one thousand fifty to one thousand two hundred dollars. Hotel rent on the pink properties is only about seven hundred fifty to eight hundred seventy-five dollars. One pink hit will not bankrupt them.

A second pink hit could bankrupt the opponent if the first strips all buildings. They would pass GO once before landing, raising cash to about two hundred thirty-four dollars. They might draw Chance cards or sell buildings preemptively during those turns. If they arrive at Virginia Avenue hotel with intact dark blue properties and that cash, they would need to sell roughly six hundred forty-one dollars in buildings to survive the eight hundred seventy-five-dollar rent. That leaves them with about fifty-nine dollars and no dark blue holdings, but their light blue properties would remain intact.

The opponent could land on St. Charles Place for seven hundred fifty dollars, leaving them with some dark blue houses and light blue properties intact. The three pink properties are clustered within four spaces of each other, so they may hit another one shortly after. This creates a dangerous kill zone where consecutive pink hits could bankrupt them.

A second pink hit would likely bankrupt the opponent even without hotels. After paying Virginia Avenue's seven hundred dollar rent, they would retain roughly four hundred dollars in light blue properties plus their two hundred thirty-four dollars cash. That combined total is below the seven hundred fifty to eight hundred seventy-five dollar rent on St. Charles or States Place.

The opponent would survive the first pink hit with roughly fifty-nine dollars and four hundred dollars in light blue properties. A second hit of seven hundred fifty dollars would leave them bankrupt, since their total liquidity drops to about four hundred fifty-nine dollars. Hotels therefore shrink the kill zone from three hits to two, which is significant because the pink properties are clustered closely together.

The opponent would survive a second pink hit without hotels, retaining about nine dollars. Hotels make it a guaranteed kill instead. The cost is three hundred dollars, leaving two thousand nine hundred sixty-six dollars in cash. Rebuilding dark blue properties later is still possible if they accumulate more funds.

The opponent cannot build before landing on the pinks. Their light blue properties are already fully upgraded with four houses and a hotel, so they have no extra houses to add. They would need cash to rebuild, but the rent would consume that cash instead.

The opponent could upgrade their light blue properties themselves. Hoteling Oriental and Vermont would cost one hundred dollars total, returning four houses each without needing bank supplies. They could also buy one house on Boardwalk to reach four houses, but they would lack the cash to hotel it afterward.

Extra houses from my hotels do not enable new construction the opponent could not already perform. The downside is negligible, so building hotels remains worthwhile. I will upgrade all three pink properties to hotels rather than just Virginia, since that maximizes rent on whichever property they land on first.

Hoteling only Virginia Avenue still guarantees a two-hit kill. The opponent would survive the first pink hit with roughly seven hundred dollars in cash and light blue properties, but the second hit of eight hundred seventy-five dollars would bankrupt them. The same outcome holds if they land on Virginia first and pay its hotel rent of eight hundred seventy-five dollars. A single hit alone cannot force bankruptcy either way.

I will build hotels on all three pink properties. This maximizes the damage of a single hit by stripping more buildings and leaving less cash for a second. I have confirmed that two thousand nine hundred sixty-six dollars in cash still covers the opponent's maximum rent against me.

Even if the opponent upgrades Boardwalk to four houses or a hotel, I can still afford the rent. The light blue hotel is well within my budget as well. Unmortgaging the railroads would cost more than the low rent they would generate, so that option is negative expected value. I am now considering whether to trade.

I will not trade. They would not exchange their winning monopolies for my mortgaged properties, and giving them cash or a Get Out of Jail Free card would help them. Selling houses would weaken my kill rent and give them buildings instead. I will build hotels on St. Charles Place, States Avenue, and Virginia Avenue.

The bank holds five houses and eleven hotels. I will return my four houses on each pink property to build hotels, since I already have four houses there. I will send a brief public message about upgrading the pinks.
